DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng has emerged as the world’s wealthiest creator of artificial intelligence models, with his estimated personal fortune reaching $55 billion after the Chinese startup completed a major fundraising round backed by some of the country’s richest business leaders.

According to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index, Liang’s wealth increased by approximately 45% following the investment, which reportedly raised around 100 billion yuan, equivalent to $15 billion.
The fundraising values DeepSeek at approximately $86 billion, placing the Hangzhou-based company among the world’s most valuable privately held artificial intelligence businesses.
The development, reported on November 24, 2026, highlights growing investor confidence in Chinese AI companies as competition intensifies with American technology firms.
However, the $55 billion figure represents an estimated valuation of Liang’s assets, largely reflecting his ownership of DeepSeek, rather than money he has personally received.

Liang Retains 67.4% Of DeepSeek Despite New Investor Funding
According to corporate registry information cited by Bloomberg, Liang’s ownership in DeepSeek declined from 81.65% in June to 67.4% following the latest fundraising.
The reduction reflects the entry of new investors who acquired stakes in the company.
Despite owning a smaller percentage, Liang’s estimated wealth increased substantially because DeepSeek’s overall valuation rose.
Bloomberg calculated the company’s implied valuation at approximately $86 billion after its latest investment round.
Liang’s net worth has more than tripled since the beginning of 2026, according to the wealth index.
The increase has placed him ahead of several prominent American AI entrepreneurs.
Bloomberg estimated OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman’s wealth at approximately $25.5 billion as of November 20, while Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei was valued at around $21.6 billion following his company’s stock market listing.
Liang’s larger estimated fortune is partly explained by his substantial ownership of DeepSeek.
Unlike founders whose stakes have been diluted through repeated investments, he continues to control more than two-thirds of his company.
However, private-company valuations are estimates based on investment transactions and financial assumptions. They do not represent guaranteed proceeds if a shareholder attempts to sell an entire stake.
Chinese Billionaires Invest In DeepSeek As AI Competition Intensifies
The latest fundraising attracted several prominent Chinese business leaders and industrial investors.
According to corporate records compiled by data platform Qichacha, at least five Chinese billionaires have acquired personal stakes in DeepSeek.
Among them is Robin Zeng, founder of battery manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology, commonly known as CATL.
Zeng holds a personal stake of approximately 0.18%, valued at $154.6 million under Bloomberg’s estimate.
His investment is separate from the participation of CATL itself.
Another investor is Zhong Shanshan, founder of bottled-water company Nongfu Spring.
Zhong, who participated in DeepSeek’s previous fundraising round, holds approximately 0.08% of the AI company, currently valued at around $70.6 million.
The participation of industrial billionaires illustrates how investment in advanced AI models is spreading beyond traditional technology companies.
Artificial intelligence increasingly influences manufacturing, energy consumption, industrial automation and digital services.
However, the public reporting does not establish that the new investors will directly control DeepSeek’s product development or business strategy.

Liang established DeepSeek in 2023 after developing an artificial intelligence research operation within Zhejiang High-Flyer Asset Management.
High-Flyer is a quantitative hedge fund that uses mathematical models, data analysis and computing technology to support investment decisions.
Liang co-founded the business with two university classmates after they began trading during the global financial crisis.
The research division eventually evolved into DeepSeek, which became known for developing advanced AI models.
The company attracted international attention by introducing competitive language models while emphasising efficient computing techniques.
Its emergence intensified debate about the cost of developing powerful AI systems and whether companies need the same level of computing expenditure as some American rivals.
DeepSeek has since attracted substantial investment as China seeks to strengthen its domestic artificial intelligence capabilities.
The new fundraising demonstrates investors’ willingness to assign considerable value to companies developing foundational AI models.

KAUST-backed startups attract $1.4 billion in total funding
November 25, 2026 by David Edwards
Startups supported by King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) have raised $1.4 billion in cumulative funding, with investment activity accelerating as companies across the University’s entrepreneurship ecosystem attract capital to develop and scale their businesses.
While KAUST has contributed approximately $77 million in funding to date, 90 percent of the portfolio’s funding comes from external sources, including $33 million from the National Technology Development Program (NTDP). This reflects the substantial investment portfolio companies are attracting from outside the University.
Sixty-six startups raised a combined $338 million in the financial year from July 2025 to June 2026. This is a year-on-year increase of more than 30 percent from the previous year, bringing total funding raised by portfolio startups to date to approximately $1.4 billion.
Among the largest reported funding rounds were $200 million for quantum computing company Pasqal and $9.2 million for cybersecurity company COGNNA, followed by Aajil (Buildnow), Iyris, and Agellus Tank Robotics.
KAUST’s portfolio includes 282 active startups with a combined valuation of $5.7 billion across artificial intelligence, enterprise software, financial technology, healthcare, agriculture and advanced technology sectors. Companies across the portfolio have generated $1.1 billion in cumulative revenue, as economic diversification remains a priority on Saudi Arabia’s national agenda.
“The success of so many of our portfolio companies is a testament to the fact that Saudi Arabia is a great place to grow and scale as a business,” said Dr. Ian Campbell, senior vice president, National Transformation Institute (NTI) at KAUST. “KAUST is a vital part of this thriving ecosystem, supporting startups to find commercialization opportunities that help bring their innovations from the lab to the market.”
KAUST combines early-stage investment with access to core laboratories and specialized facilities to help founders build and develop their companies. KAUST leverages longstanding impact partnerships with SAB, NTDP and NIDLP, as well as in-Kingdom venture capital firms and institutional partners to commercialize and localize technologies through programs like TAQADAM, NextEra, ScaleX, the KAUST Venture Studio program and the KAUST 4th Industrial Revolution Center.
“KAUST spinouts and spin-ins are delivering solutions to a wide range of real-world issues and driving growth as they do so,” said Haitham Al Humsi, director of innovation ecosystem development at KAUST.
“The Venture Studio is a new initiative that we are expanding. It focuses on building startup ventures and commercializing intellectual property aligned with the Kingdom’s strategic priority areas from the start and allows us to bring new materials, new industrial processes, and sensor-based healthcare innovations to the market.”
The KAUST Research and Technology Park connects startups with KAUST’s researchers, faculty, talent and facilities, and introduces them to companies across the Kingdom, as well as anchors international scaleups into the KAUST R&D ecosystem. These connections help startups draw on KAUST’s research capabilities, test technologies and develop commercial expansion.
Examples within the portfolio include iStoria and Faheem in education, Kestrl and EdfaPay in finance, and Cura and Atomica AI in healthcare. Food-related businesses include Barakah and Aqua Development, while TileGreen and Edama feature among companies working in waste reduction, recycling or reuse.
This latest annual assessment of the KAUST entrepreneurship portfolio applies standard methodologies, covering 282 active startups, using self-reported data from 83 percent of companies.
By understanding where value and success are being delivered, KAUST can determine where further development of its ecosystem is required, supporting broader innovation expansion and attracting investment to the Kingdom.

RiverStone raises $400m in debt markets with first legacy RT1 issuance
RiverStone becomes the first legacy run-off insurer to tap RT1 capital markets under Solvency II
REINSURANCE NEWS
By
Mark Rosanes
Nov 25, 2026
Share
RiverStone International has completed a US$400 million Restricted Tier 1 capital issuance, becoming what it describes as the first legacy run-off insurer to access an instrument that European live-market insurers have used for years to optimize their Solvency II capital structures. The notes carry a coupon of 9.875% and qualify as RT1 regulatory capital under Solvency II. They have been admitted to trading on the International Securities Market (ISM) of the London Stock Exchange.
The transaction is RiverStone's largest public debt issuance to date and its second capital markets deal in 2026, following a US$150 million Tier 2 issuance in April. Combined, the two transactions bring total public debt raised this year to US$550 million. Morgan Stanley acted as sole global coordinator, with Barclays, Goldman Sachs International, Lloyds Bank Corporate Markets, and Morgan Stanley as joint lead managers, and CVC Capital Markets as co-manager.
Get the latest reinsurance news direct to your inbox twice a week. Sign up here
A new instrument for a run-off balance sheet
RT1 instruments are perpetual, deeply subordinated notes that sit at the highest-risk end of an insurer's capital stack. Under Solvency II, they qualify as Tier 1 capital but are restricted to no more than 20% of total Tier 1. Their key feature is loss absorbency. Distributions can be cancelled and principal repayment suspended if the issuer breaches its solvency capital requirement.
Live-market European insurers, including Legal and General and Phoenix Group Holdings, have used RT1 instruments to manage their Solvency II capital ratios. That a run-off specialist has accessed the same market is new.
The 9.875% coupon reflects how debt investors price the structural differences between a run-off business and a live underwriter. A legacy acquirer does not generate new premium income. Its earnings come from reserve releases, investment returns, and transaction margins. That profile is less familiar to fixed-income investors, and the coupon captures the premium they require for the exposure.
Capital built for deal velocity
The rationale for the issuance becomes clearer in the context of RiverStone's 2026 transaction pace. The firm has completed a US$1.6 billion loss portfolio transfer with QBE Insurance Group , taken on approximately US$400 million of legacy reinsurance liabilities from SiriusPoint , completed a $325 million LPT with Clear Spring Property and Casualty, made its ILS market debut through a Leadenhall Capital Partners transaction, and expanded into Australia.
Large LPT transactions require acquirers to deploy capital quickly once a deal is agreed, and the ability to draw on a diversified capital structure rather than retained earnings alone gives RiverStone more capacity to pursue multiple transactions concurrently.
Andy Creed, group president and group chief financial officer of RiverStone, said the issuance "reflects the strength of RiverStone's financial position, our disciplined approach to capital management and the continued development of our global platform," adding that the additional financial flexibility would support the group "as we continue to pursue attractive opportunities across the global legacy market."
A maturing market
RiverStone's ILS debut through the Leadenhall transaction in late October 2026 extended that approach, adding alternative capital to the mix alongside its public debt program. The repeat-seller dynamic that now defines the legacy market , where carriers treat LPTs as recurring capital management tools rather than one-off exits, requires acquirers to maintain standing capacity rather than raising it deal by deal. The RT1 issuance, alongside the April Tier 2, is evidence that RiverStone is building that kind of balance sheet.
For cedants considering legacy transactions, the depth of RiverStone's capital structure is now a verifiable fact rather than an assumption, which changes the conversation around counterparty certainty for large or complex deals.

candidates.text:
Tucows’ Ting Fiber Sale Would Move $301.5 Million In Securitized Debt Off Its Balance Sheet
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 12:31 PM
Tucows’ Ting Fiber Sale Would Move $301.5 Million In Securitized Debt Off Its Balance Sheet
Tucows subsidiary Ting Fiber has agreed to sell Ting Holdco, which owns Ting’s fiber markets and their securitized financing facility, to Clearwave for nominal cash consideration. Approximately $301.5 million in non-recourse securitized notes will remain with Ting Holdco. Tucows expects to remove that debt from its consolidated balance sheet at closing.
Tucows Retains Ting’s Partner Markets
Tucows will contribute $3 million in cash to Simply Bits, which will remain part of Ting Holdco. A previous commitment to invest up to $12.5 million in Ting will end when the transaction closes. Tucows will retain Ting’s partner markets.
A Tucows subsidiary will provide transition services for nine months after closing, with Clearwave able to extend the period by up to two months. The companies said customer service, pricing, billing and support will continue as before during the transition.
Tucows expects the sale to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to conditions including Federal Communications Commission and state utility approvals, noteholder consents and rating agency confirmations. The company expects its remaining debt to consist primarily of its syndicated credit facility, which had $184.4 million in principal outstanding as of September 30, 2026. Its 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance, which excludes Ting, remains unchanged.
KEY QUOTE
“This agreement is a key outcome we have been working toward since we began the Ting strategic process. Upon closing, it is expected to remove more than $300 million in principal amount of securitized debt and the capital demands that came with building fiber networks. What will remain is a simpler, more focused business that we expect to generate cash more consistently: a portfolio of recurring-revenue businesses, led by Tucows Domains and Wavelo, with the flexibility to invest where we see the best returns. Greater flexibility carries an obligation to be disciplined, and Tucows’ job now is to put it to work in ways that compound value per share over time. I want to thank the Ting team for building a valuable business, and for their continued care for customers through the transition.”
Dave Woroch, Chief Executive Officer Of Tucows

Adani Airport Holdings Signs ₹2,790 Crore (US$300 Million) Equity Deal At An $18 Billion Valuation
Adani Airport Holdings has signed a binding agreement to raise ₹2,790 crore (US$300 million) from funds and affiliates of 360 ONE Alternates Asset Management, bringing its announced equity raise to US$1.35 billion.

Sea Box Receives $216.4 Million Army Vehicle For Expandable Maintenance Shelters
Sea Box has received a $216.36 million firm-fixed-price indefinite-delivery Army contract to supply one-sided expandable shelters for two maintenance shop programs.

candidates.text:
Arch MI Secures $202.5 Million In Reinsurance Through Bellemeade Transaction
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 1:06 PM
Arch MI Secures $202.5 Million In Reinsurance Through Bellemeade Transaction
Arch Mortgage Insurance Company has secured $202.5 million in indemnity reinsurance covering a pool representing approximately $55 billion in mortgages through Bellemeade Re 2026-1, a special-purpose reinsurer.
The transaction closed November 24 and combines approximately $162 million in insurance-linked notes with $40.5 million in direct reinsurance.
The coverage primarily relates to mortgage insurance policies issued by Arch MI and its affiliates from September 2025 through October 2026. The $55 billion figure represents the underlying mortgage pool, while $202.5 million is the reinsurance protection obtained.
Five Note Classes Support Risk Transfer
Bellemeade Re 2026-1 is funding its reinsurance obligations through five classes of amortizing notes, each with a 10-year legal final maturity.
The issuance includes approximately $45.94 million in Class M-1A notes paying one-month SOFR plus 1.50% and $45.94 million in Class M-1B notes paying SOFR plus 2%.
The remaining classes comprise approximately $36.27 million in Class M-1C notes at SOFR plus 2.50%, $19.34 million in Class M-2 notes at SOFR plus 3%, and $14.51 million in Class B-1 notes at SOFR plus 4.50%.
Morningstar DBRS assigned ratings ranging from BBB (low)(sf) for Class M-1A to B (sf) for Class B-1. An additional $40.503 million was placed with a panel of reinsurers.
Bellemeade Program Reaches 23 Transactions
The deal is Arch’s first mortgage insurance-linked note transaction of 2026. Since launching the Bellemeade program in 2015, the company has completed 23 transactions securing nearly $10 billion in indemnity reinsurance.
Arch MI described the program as an important component of its risk and capital management strategy, with the latest transaction’s amortization structure aligned with its PMIERs capital requirements.
Headquartered in Greensboro, North Carolina, Arch MI is a wholly owned subsidiary of Arch Capital Group. Its flagship insurer is licensed to write mortgage insurance in all 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico.
KEY QUOTES
“We have issued at least one Bellemeade transaction a year since 2015, and we remain committed to the program as an important part of Arch’s risk and capital management strategy.”
“We are very pleased with the execution of this transaction. Strong investor engagement allowed us to achieve attractive execution across the capital structure, while maintaining an amortization structure aligned with our PMIERs capital requirements.”
Jennifer Weiss, Vice President Of Structured Capital And Reinsurance At Arch MI

E.F. Hutton Advises Poco Loco Holdings Group on $188.2 Million Financing
November 25, 2026
E.F. Hutton & Co. , a New York-based investment bank and broker-dealer, served as exclusive financial advisor to Poco Loco Holdings Group LLC on an approximately $188.2 million financing transaction comprising mortgage financing, land sale-leaseback and build-to-suit financing arrangements.
The transaction will enable Poco Loco to unlock capital from its existing real estate portfolio, enhance liquidity and support future development, expansion initiatives and construction of multiple retail locations.
Poco Loco is a family-owned, Texas-based Hispanic grocery and convenience retail operator serving communities across Central and South Texas.
The company has grown from a single neighborhood grocery store into a diversified retail platform encompassing full-service supermarkets, meat markets, convenience stores and gas stations.
Supported by more than 1,000 employees, Poco Loco specializes in providing fresh, authentic and affordable groceries to the communities it serves.
The financing combines multiple real estate-backed funding structures, allowing Poco Loco to optimize its property holdings while securing capital to support its long-term expansion strategy.
“Convenience and fuel operators often hold valuable real estate, and financing it well takes a structure that reflects both the property and the business that operates on it,” said Duncan B. Swanston , president of E.F. Hutton.
“We are pleased to have advised Poco Loco on this financing and look forward to supporting the company as it continues to grow.”
The transaction highlights E.F. Hutton’s private credit capabilities, which include structuring and arranging customized financing solutions across direct lending, mezzanine financing, real estate-backed financing and structured credit.
The individual financing amounts, participating lenders and other transaction terms were not disclosed.
Headquartered in New York City, E.F. Hutton provides investment banking, financial advisory, capital raising and financing services to corporations, financial sponsors and institutional investors across the United States, Europe, the Middle East, Asia and Latin America.
The $188.2 million financing positions Poco Loco to expand its retail footprint while leveraging the value of its existing real estate assets to support continued growth across Texas.

Sabre Systems Receives $155.7 Million Increase To Navy Engineering Support Ceiling
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 12:16 PM
Sabre Systems Receives $155.7 Million Increase To Navy Engineering Support Ceiling
Sabre Systems received a $155.69 million increase to the labor-cost ceiling on an existing Naval Air Systems Command engineering support contract.
The modification raises the ceiling from $499.92 million to $655.61 million while leaving the fee unchanged. The increase expands the contract’s available labor-cost capacity rather than representing an immediate funding obligation.
The indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract supports Naval Air Systems Command program offices with systems engineering, research and development, technical baseline work and engineering assessments.

Epochal launches with $100M to help developers train predictive AI models
by Maria Deutscher
Artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc. launched today with $100 million in funding.
The capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp. He established Epochal earlier this year with two other xAI co-founders, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss. The company’s staff also includes former researchers from Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Google DeepMind.
Epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal. According to the company, it enables developers to train AI models that can predict future events. The service does so by providing models with access to historical web data from the past 30 years.
If a bank wishes to train an AI that can predict quarterly earnings, it could use the service to fetch financial results from the first three quarters of 2025. It could then ask the AI to estimate fourth-quarter results from the same year.
After the model generates its predictions, developers can compare them against real fourth-quarter earnings to check the model’s accuracy. They can make adjustments if necessary and then repeat the training workflow until the model starts generating accurate forecasts.
The Epochal Time Portal features more than 1 trillion historical web pages on launch. Each entry includes a timestamp that indicates when it was created. According to the company, its timestamps make it possible to track how a web page changed over time.
AI models access the content through a purpose-built search engine. It enables them to specify the time periods from which they wish to retrieve web pages. According to Epochal, its platform provides one-minute granularity for the most frequently updated pages.
Like consumer search engines, the Epochal Time Portal prioritizes the web pages that are most relevant to each given query. The difference is that it considers web pages’ creation date when evaluating relevance. If a query contains the term “Meta” but asks for pages created before 2021, the year Facebook Inc. rebranded, the Epochal Time Portal will not bring up pages that relate to the social networking giant.
Today’s frontier models can determine that they’re being trained on historical data rather than up-to-date information. For example, a model might compare the creation date of a web page to the virtual clock of the operating system on which it deployed. Such discrepancies can lower the effectiveness of training runs.
According to Epochal, its service mitigates the issue by deploying AI models in sandboxes synced to their training data. If a company is training a model on we pages from 2025, the Epochal Time Portal will run it on a Linux version from that year. It applies the same precautions to the software tools and programming language versions that models use.
The Epochal Time Portal is initially available in a single free tier with low usage limits. Epochal plans to follow up the launch by sharing the results of several AI experiments that its researchers have carried out using the service.

candidates.title: AI Peptide Drug Lab Capable Raises $38M Seed to Automate Drug Discovery
candidates.snippet: AI Peptide Drug Lab Capable Raises $38M Seed to Automate Drug Discovery Wowtale
candidates.text:
Finding and refining a single drug candidate can take years. Capable , a San Francisco biotech, wants to cut that to months with a lab where AI designs molecules, automated equipment synthesizes them and cells and mice test them straight away. Its first drug candidate is a wakefulness peptide meant to reduce sleep and extend time awake. The company has raised a $38 million seed round.
What Capable sells is not software or data but drugs. It finds its own candidates and takes them through animal testing, and it is preparing both to move a candidate into the clinic and to hand assets to pharma companies through deals. Peptides are drugs built as short chains of amino acids, small pieces of protein. Capable makes peptide and nucleotide therapeutics on automated synthesis equipment, and its in-house research AI agent designs candidates by pulling specialized models, such as a potency predictor, off the shelf like tools. The company says it has built a lab that can go from AI design to experimental data in 24 hours.
Capable disclosed the seed round on its company blog on October 16 (US time). Cathay Innovation , Abstract Ventures, Fidji Simo, Joe Betts-LaCroix and Andrej Karpathy, among others, took part, bringing total funding to $50 million. Karpathy is the OpenAI co-founder who joined Anthropic in May. According to startup data firm Dealroom, the valuation and lead investor were not disclosed. Capable will use the money to scale its lab and platform. It grew from 2,000 square feet to 22,500 square feet in about three weeks and moved to Mission Bay, near UCSF.
Its most advanced program is CAPABLE-002, a wakefulness drug candidate. The company produced its first batch, 180 grams, enough to dose hundreds of rats, dozens of dogs and a few dozen humans. The compound is entering preclinical safety testing, in which a drug is dosed repeatedly in a rodent and a non-rodent species while tissues and hundreds of biomarkers are examined, and Capable plans to dose the first dogs within a few weeks. In early mouse experiments it cut sleep by 30% to 50%. Efficacy and safety in people remain unproven.
The company has already found a follow-up molecule. It is similarly potent but 70% smaller, at roughly 750 daltons, which raises hopes of an oral drug after further optimization. It relies heavily on non-canonical amino acids, which are rare in nature, and the follow-up molecule is about 80% non-canonical. Because both versions are highly potent on the same pathway, the safety study will continue, and Capable will decide whether to take version one into the clinic or reset the timeline for a better version two.
The second program is an “exercise mimetic,” a drug meant to reproduce some benefits of exercise on the heart, liver, kidneys, brain and muscle preservation. The research agent has designed about 500 first candidates, and Capable wants a development candidate within three or four months, against two to five years for comparable stages in pharma, by its own comparison.
Automation drives the speed. Automated cell assays raised the number of compounds tested per day by more than 10 times and cut run-to-run scatter from 6% to about 1.75%, and drying can now handle up to 1,152 compounds at once. Steven Cao, formerly of Cognition and Redwood Research, joined with experience training large models, while Shane Lafayette, a former director of business development at sleep drug developer Centessa, and UCSF and Gladstone professor Vijay Ramani advise.
Sleep and wakefulness medicine entered a new phase this year. In August, Takeda won FDA approval for Orzeyful (oveporexton) for narcolepsy type 1, the first drug of its kind that activates the orexin receptor, which governs wakefulness signals in the brain. Capable has not said whether it uses the same approach.
Startups that pair AI with laboratories are multiplying, but they do different jobs. Capable handles AI design, synthesis, animal testing and its own drug candidates. Leash Biosciences positions itself as infrastructure selling experimental environments and data to other AI developers. Lila Sciences builds autonomous labs where AI runs experiments on drugs, catalysts and materials, and Periodic Labs focuses on discovering materials such as superconductors. Unlike them, Capable has tuned its synthesis line to a single field, peptide drugs. On the model side, Chai Discovery and Isomorphic Labs lead with AI that designs new molecules. Among companies chasing oral peptide drugs, Ambrosia Biosciences raised $100 million for a next-generation oral obesity treatment. Wowtale’s AI biotech landscape (in Korean) maps the wider field.

Japanese humanoid robotics startup Atom has signed loan agreements totaling about $28.3 million with three major Japanese banks to support development of its physical AI technology and prepare for mass production of humanoid robots.
Tokyo-based Atom is developing both a two-armed, bipedal humanoid robot and its own physical AI platform model, working on the hardware and software together so its robots can adapt to different working environments.

Lute's touch-focused models learn physical properties like grip force and slipping that vision alone cannot capture.
Lute-0 matched the leading open-source robot model using about one-twentieth of the data.
Lute's software turns each customer deployment into training data that carries learning across sites.
OTB Ventures announced on November 25, 2026 that it co-led a seed round for robotics startup Lute alongside FORWARD.one, bringing the company’s combined pre-seed and seed funding to $20 million. The capital will expand tactile data collection, improve Lute’s models and support customer deployments.
Seedcamp, Credo Ventures, Naval Ravikant, Inovo VC, ff Venture Capital and Borusan Ventures also participated. Lute is developing touch-focused foundation models and deployment software for robots, with the goal of making physical AI dependable in customer operations.
Touch Sensors Supply a Different Training Signal
Robots that depend mainly on vision can miss critical properties of the objects they handle. Grip force, the earliest signs of slipping, and softness or fragility all concern contact rather than appearance. Lute is building a new family of foundation models around touch to supply that additional signal.
To gather the necessary data, Lute co-designed compact, soft, skin-like touch sensors with a partner and incorporated them into a portable data-collection setup. Its first model, Lute-0, learns from video how scenes change and converts that learning into robot actions.
OTB reports that Lute-0 matched Pi0.5, which it describes as the leading open-source robot model, on dexterous tasks after pre-training with about one-twentieth of the data and one-quarter of the training steps.
Software Turns Deployments Into Training Data
Lute’s technology is not tied to one hardware platform and is designed for system integrators, the companies that put robots into operation. It guides them through hardware selection, task definition and on-site retraining, particularly where they want to deploy AI-driven robots without an in-house machine-learning team.
Its software monitors each task, pauses when something goes wrong and transfers control to a remote operator. Successful tasks and corrected failures then become training data, with learning intended to carry from one site to the next. This gives each deployment two roles: completing customer work and generating data for later training.
OTB says that, ten months after starting, Lute is deployed at what it calls Europe’s largest automotive retail distributor, a business with $6 billion in annual revenue. Its models also operate in hospital corridors, and Lute is working on site with large retailers.
Founders Combine AI and Robotics Experience
Chief executive Paweł Budzianowski holds a machine-learning PhD from Cambridge and previously led PolyAI’s AI team, where he worked on taking conversational AI from research into production for global brands. He also co-founded K-Scale Labs, which built affordable open-source humanoid robots.
Chief technology officer Krzysztof Walas was an associate professor at Poznań University of Technology and headed the Physical Interaction Robotics team at IDEAS NCBR. His work covered tactile sensing, dexterous manipulation and cable handling; he also advised Nomagic and served on the board of the European AI, Data and Robotics Association.
The 16-person team is split between Warsaw and the Bay Area and includes four PhDs and two Informatics Olympiad laureates.
OTB’s investment thesis treats dependable operation at customer sites as a source of value in its own right, alongside advances in model capability. For Lute, the ability to carry lessons from one deployment to the next is what connects that thesis to its product.

UAE’s Sooner Raises $20M Seed to Help Dubai Renters Buy Homes With 10% Down
Sooner raises a $20M seed round, $5M equity led by Nuwa Capital and a $15M debt facility, to cut first-time buyers' upfront down payment in Dubai.
By Abdelrahman Amr 25 November 2026 · 4 min read
Summary
Sooner has announced a $20 million seed round for its down payment platform.
Nuwa Capital led $5 million in equity, with 500 Global and others joining.
Amwal Capital Partners provided a $15 million Shariah-compliant debt facility.
Buyers pay 10% upfront instead of 20%, with the rest over 60 monthly instalments.
The startup plans to launch a home equity line of credit in 2027.
Sooner, a UAE down payment support platform licensed by the Dubai Land Department, has announced a $20 million seed round. The package combines $5 million in equity led by Nuwa Capital with a $15 million Shariah-compliant debt facility from Amwal Capital Partners, which gives the startup the capacity to support $272 million of home purchases in 2027.
Joining Nuwa Capital on the equity side are 500 Global, Annex Investments, Plus VC, Serkal Group, Axeed Group, 21Ventures, Iliad Partners and angel investors, including operators from AWS, Lean Technologies and Sarwa.
The problem Sooner is going after is a familiar one. First-time homebuyers in Dubai usually have to find a 20% down payment plus 7 to 10% in closing fees, all in cash, upfront. Together that comes to 27 to 30% of the price: about $230,000 (AED 850K) on an $800,000 (AED 3M) home, against roughly 6 to 10% in the United States and the United Kingdom.
Most of these buyers can afford the monthly mortgage payments. What holds them back is the cash on day one.
Sooner's model changes that maths. Buyers pick from Sooner-compatible homes and pay 10% instead of 20% upfront, with the remainder spread over 60 equal Shariah-compliant monthly instalments. They also get access to first-time homebuyer mortgages from all leading UAE banks, with a lowest mortgage rate guarantee. The company says its mission starts with helping renters become homeowners about two years sooner.
The early numbers are worth a look. Since its launch in July 2026, Sooner has received about 9,000 applications, representing $4.5 billion in buying demand, and has already supported around $10 million of home purchases.
The founding team will be familiar to anyone who follows the Gulf's fintech scene. CEO Mohammed Aziz exited his payments company Pluto to Tamara and was the first UAE-based founder to be backed by Y Combinator. Gabriel García Leyva launched rent now pay later at Keyper, and Vlad Cherevkov previously led products at Revolut and Deel.
"Every year a first-time buyer spends saving for a down payment, which is a year of rent paid towards someone else's mortgage. We are solving that problem and making sure that people in the UAE can realise their dream of home ownership sooner," said Mohammed Aziz, CEO and co-founder of Sooner.
Aziz said he went through the problem himself, saving towards the down payment on his first family home while also paying rent. García Leyva, for his part, said the UAE market "has been historically undercredited and investor-focused" and is now ripe for a shift to end-user homeowners. He added that Sooner uses technology to deliver instant mortgage and down payment pre-approvals, helping customers get keys in hand in as little as two weeks.
Next up is a second product. In 2027, Sooner plans to launch what it describes as the UAE's first Home Equity Line of Credit (HELOC), allowing existing homeowners to unlock value from their current properties to secure financing for a new home. It is modelled on America's largest HELOC platforms, publicly listed Figure and Aven, a $2.2 billion unicorn. The company puts the UAE alone at a $4.1 billion revenue opportunity for its products and plans to expand to structurally similar markets, regionally and internationally.
The backers are reading the same trend. "Down payment support and home equity release are standard in developed housing markets and still largely missing in the Gulf," said Arnav Danthi, partner at Nuwa Capital. Sharif Eid, Head of Fixed Income at Amwal Capital Partners, said the Dubai property story is shifting from investor speculation to resident ownership, and that the down payment is the biggest barrier to ownership, "yet it measures savings, not affordability".
The timing fits. Residential mortgage lending in Dubai hit a record $5.9 billion in the third quarter of 2026, according to Cavendish Maxwell, and Dubai's Real Estate Sector Strategy 2033 targets a home-ownership rate of 33%. Around Arageek, we often talk about fintech moving beyond payments into bigger-ticket lending, and I reckon housing is where that gets properly interesting. That said, pairing equity with a large debt facility at seed stage means execution and credit discipline will matter as much as demand. If Sooner gets that right, it could make the leap from renter to owner a lot less of a faff for the region's salaried professionals.

Santa Clara Family Health Plan invests $19.2 million to help Medi-Cal members retain healthcare coverage
News provided by
Santa Clara Family Health Plan
Nov 25, 2026, 15:06 ET

Funding expands outreach, renewal assistance, and community partnerships as new Medicaid requirements take effect
SAN JOSÉ , Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Santa Clara Family Health Plan (SCFHP) has committed $19.2 million over the next two years to help Medi-Cal members maintain their healthcare coverage as significant state and federal Medicaid policy changes take effect in January 2027. The investment represents one of the largest local efforts to support coverage retention and ensure residents remain connected to critical healthcare services.
Approved by the SCFHP Governing Board on October 22, the funding will strengthen community outreach, expand renewal assistance, and increase access to personalized support to help prevent eligible members from losing their healthcare coverage.
"No one should lose healthcare coverage because they missed a form, didn't understand a new requirement, or couldn't get help navigating the system," Chris Turner, SCFHP Chief Operating Officer said. "This investment reflects our commitment to removing barriers and helping our members navigate changes that could affect their healthcare. We want every eligible member to remain covered and connected to the care they need."
The cornerstone of the $19.2 million investment is a $15 million commitment to Valley Health Foundation (VHF) to advance the work of the Santa Clara County Coverage Retention Collaborative. Since April, Santa Clara Family Health Plan has partnered with VHF, the County of Santa Clara agencies, safety-net healthcare providers, and community-based organizations to develop a shared approach to supporting individuals in maintaining continuous Medi-Cal enrollment. SCFHP's contribution to VHF will establish a grant program for community-based organizations, provide continued funding for community clinic patient enrollment, and launch a coordinated public information campaign. Learn more about the Coverage Retention Collaborative at: www.valleyhealthfoundtion.org/Coverage
"The partnership was forged on a shared belief that a coordinated, public-non-profit-community-philanthropy effort can make significant progress in reducing coverage losses, saving thousands of local families from hardship, and preserving essential safety-net health services," Michael Elliott, VHF President and Executive Director, said.
These investments come in response to H.R. 1, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which introduces significant changes to Medicaid (Medi-Cal in California), including new work and community engagement requirements for certain adults, more frequent eligibility renewals for some beneficiaries, and additional administrative requirements. These changes could create new challenges for Medi-Cal members trying to maintain their healthcare coverage and access essential healthcare services.
In addition to the funding for VHF, SCFHP will invest $4.2 million in four key initiatives designed to strengthen support for its members. The largest portion, $3 million, will expand billable Medi-Cal Community Health Worker (CHW) services, increasing outreach and personalized assistance to help members navigate the Medi-Cal renewal process. This funding will enable SCFHP's network of contracted CHW providers to conduct outreach that may not qualify for reimbursement under current billing requirements.
An additional $400,000 will be invested in AI technology that will help members understand renewal requirements, receive timely reminders, and complete renewal forms. Building on SCFHP's existing AI chatbot Scout, these enhancements will create more opportunities for members to receive assistance throughout the renewal process.
Another $400,000 will support increased staffing at SCFHP's Blanca Alvarado and South County Community Resource Centers. For many members, these centers are trusted places to turn for guidance, resources, and one-on-one support, helping them overcome language, technology, and administrative barriers that could otherwise put their healthcare coverage at risk. By increasing staffing, SCFHP will be able to serve more members face-to-face.
The remaining $400,000 will fund a new partnership with the County Social Services Agency Department of Enrollment and Benefits Services, bringing their staff to SCFHP Community Resource Centers. By co-locating services, members will gain access to technical support with renewals in a trusted setting, reducing delays and helping resolve complex coverage issues more quickly.
As new Medicaid requirements reshape the coverage landscape, SCFHP is helping to mobilize resources across the county to ensure eligible residents do not lose healthcare coverage because of administrative barriers. Through expanded outreach, enhanced technology, strengthened community partnerships, and direct enrollment support, SCFHP is working to help members stay covered, stay informed, and stay connected to care. To learn more about Medi-Cal changes, visit https://www.scfhp.com/medi-cal-changes/ .
About Santa Clara Family Health Plan
Santa Clara Family Health Plan (SCFHP) is a local, community-based health plan dedicated to creating opportunities for better health and wellness for all. In partnership with providers and community organizations since 1997, SCFHP works to ensure everyone in Santa Clara County has access to equitable, high-quality health care. With a strong commitment to integrity, outstanding service, and support for the community, SCFHP serves more than 270,000 people through its Medi-Cal and Medicare health plans. candidates.title: Every raises $17.5 million at $110 million valuation, betting venture-backed media can work
candidates.snippet: Every raises $17.5 million at $110 million valuation, betting venture-backed media can work Fortune
candidates.text:
Ask Dan Shipper how often venture-backed media startups succeed, and he’s candid.
Recommended Video
“My feeling about the history of media companies taking venture capital is that it doesn’t go very well,” he said. In other words, it usually doesn’t work out, I suggest. “It works out never, actually,” laughs Shipper, founder of AI-focused media and software company Every.
Shipper’s right: VC-backed media startups of yesteryear have frequently tanked in spectacular fashion, from The Messenger and Vice to Ozy Media and Quibi. But Shipper is betting that Every—currently with about 130,000 unpaid subscribers and almost 10,000 paid—can play by its own rules and ultimately win its own game.
Hence, the fundraise: Every recently raised $17.5 million in Series A funding, at a $110 million post-money valuation, Fortune has exclusively learned. IA Ventures’s Jesse Beyroutey led the round, with Betaworks and The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson joining, among others. Shipper, 35, will retain full control of the company, and is changing his title to “Philosopher King,” which I rib him about. He good-naturedly says the change is semiotic.
“The really important thing about taking the money for me was that we’d do it in a way that allows us to achieve our goals… and do it in a way that doesn’t require us to sacrifice our soul or the things about the company that I love deeply,” said Shipper. “I think of changing my title as a symbolic thing. If this was a normal venture capital deal, that would be completely off the table and ridiculous.”
And this isn’t a normal venture deal, in a couple of ways. First, Every is a media company. With its neoclassical pop art aesthetic, Every has a multi-pronged business model: Its writing serves a professional audience seeking to become “AI-native,” while the 35-person company also provides consulting services to large companies and produces conferences (I recently interviewed Shipper at Every’s Thesis: 2027 conference in Brooklyn). Second, Shipper didn’t raise in a standard startup process: IA’s Beyroutey and Shipper are close friends (they went to college together) and Shipper went straight to Beyroutey.
“I didn’t shop the deal,” said Shipper. “I went to someone I deeply trust, who understands the business deeply, who understands exactly what I want to do with it, and has put me in the position where I make all the decisions to build the company in the way that I want to build it,” Shipper said. “I think that’s the only way to build a business like this, because this is a very unique shape. It’s a media company and a technology company, kind of smushed together.”
Shipper started Every in 2020, about six years after exiting his first startup, co-browsing company Firefly, in 2014 ( the acquisition came right as he was graduating college ). He spent the intervening years finding the right next thing. Every became the answer, in part because it addressed a number of questions that Shipper had been asking throughout his life. For one, he’d long felt tension between writing and entrepreneurship (at Every he could be both). He’d also been interested in tech since he was a kid.
“I thought a lot about why Microsoft and Windows had worked, and one of the big reasons is that they came during a hardware platform shift, from mainframes to PCs,” said Shipper. “They started building operating systems for that, and that’s always a really big opportunity…. And I thought: I wonder what my platform shift is going to be?”
Shipper and Every are all-in on AI, and the company is built to help people understand how they can actually use AI, in their jobs and their lives.
“I think too few companies are trying to do that,” said Shipper. “Too many companies are trying to build the machine god or are worrying about Armageddon, and I’m not…. I would expect improvements we’re seeing [in AI] to continue, and I would expect there to be a gap between the improvements that you see on the charts and how well those improvements translate into actually better work by people (and that people at companies are proud of). Our job is to fill that gap.”
Shipper is optimistic that AI won’t replace humans at work, a common fear and feature of AI discourse.
“The narrative is ‘it’s so over for humans’, and I think that’s exactly wrong,” he said. “That relies on this sleight of hand where you forget that humans are the ones who make these things, and humans are the ones that prompt these things—and decide what’s valuable and what’s not.”
In some sense, Shipper expects AI to eventually blur into the background, much in the same way we don’t really say “I used the Internet.”
“Ultimately, I think the technology and the model advances will disappear, and we’ll actually just think about the humans that did it,” said Shipper. “Asking if Claude did it will be like asking if you used your laptop. ‘Did your laptop do it?’ No, you did it.”
Happy Thanksgiving and we’ll see you again on Monday.

Northrop Grumman Receives $16.4 Million Navy Order For International E-2 Aircraft Support
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 12:29 PM
Northrop Grumman Receives $16.4 Million Navy Order For International E-2 Aircraft Support
Northrop Grumman Systems received a $16.41 million Navy order to provide in-service and technical support for E-2C and E-2D aircraft operated by foreign military sales customers.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee order supports customers in France, Japan, Taiwan and Egypt. It covers requirements shared across participating customers alongside country-specific support.
The award establishes a support effort extending through October 2033, the expected completion date.
Foreign Military Sales Funding Supports Initial Work
The Navy obligated $6.65 million in foreign military sales funds when it issued the order. That initial obligation represents approximately 40.5% of the announced order value.
The funding committed at award is therefore distinct from the full $16.41 million value. The provided details do not specify a schedule for additional obligations or allocate funding among the four customers.
Most Work Will Take Place In Florida
Northrop Grumman will perform approximately 64% of the work in Melbourne, Florida.
The remaining work will take place across customer locations: Lorient and Cuers in France; Misawa and Tokyo in Japan; Pingtung, Taiwan; and Cairo, Egypt.
The geographic distribution combines a majority of support activity in the United States with work performed in the countries operating the aircraft. The notice does not provide separate percentages for each overseas location.
Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, issued order N0001927F1065 under basic ordering agreement N0001925G0003. The order uses that existing agreement to address the shared and country-specific aircraft support requirements.

Vero Security has raised $11 mn in seed funding to develop its AI Security Engineering platform, which automates security management and policy enforcement across enterprise AI tools and agents.
The funding round was led by TLV Partners, with participation from GTM Capital, Maple Capital and angel investors. Founded in 2025, Vero already serves several Fortune 500 companies.
Vero Security has secured $11 mn in seed funding led by TLV Partners, with participation from GTM Capital, Maple Capital and angel investors.
Its AI Security Engineering platform automates security policy enforcement, risk remediation and runtime protection across enterprise AI tools and agents.
Research from IANS and Artico Search found that 65% of companies with at least $10 bn in revenue had appointed an AI security leader, but only 18% had established a dedicated role.
The platform addresses the operational demands of enterprise AI security teams. Security professionals define policies, which Vero converts into enforceable controls, automatically adjusting protections as AI vendors modify their products and escalating decisions that require human judgment.
The company is also launching AISecurityEngineering.org, an open professional community dedicated to AI security engineering.
AI Security Engineering emerges as a dedicated enterprise discipline
Research from IANS and Artico Search found that 65% of companies generating at least $10 bn in annual revenue had assigned responsibility for AI security to a designated leader. Only 18% had established a dedicated position, with other organizations incorporating AI security into existing leadership responsibilities.
Employees are adopting new AI applications and autonomous agents, connecting them to enterprise infrastructure and granting permissions to access sensitive information and execute actions.
AI vendors regularly introduce new models, capabilities, plugins and integrations, potentially changing the security implications of previously approved configurations.
Elad Tessler, co-founder and CEO of Vero Security, said Vero is working with enterprise AI security leaders to develop technology that maintains protections as AI capabilities change, allowing security professionals to concentrate on decisions requiring human intervention.
CISOs have seen enough dashboards and tables that tell their teams what’s wrong and leave the work to them. AI Security Engineering deserves a better operating model, designed for AI rather than borrowed from other areas of securit.
Elad Tessler, Vero Security
AI security professionals are defining their responsibilities with relatively few established operating procedures or formal training programs. Through AISecurityEngineering.org, Vero plans to provide an open knowledge center offering practical field guides, workshops and the ASE professional credential track.
AI runtime security and automated policy enforcement
Vero’s platform incorporates an AI Runtime Governor that enforces security policies during AI execution. Its runtime controls inspect supported prompts, tool calls and agent actions, applying approved restrictions when an action is attempted.
The technology can prevent coding agents from accessing sensitive credentials without authorization, block actions that violate corporate security policies and prevent malicious skills or prompt injection attacks from triggering unauthorized behavior.
Security controls operate during execution rather than relying on subsequent manual review. Vero integrates with existing enterprise endpoint, identity, AI and cybersecurity systems, eliminating the need for employees to install additional software.
The platform combines continuous discovery, security analysis and runtime enforcement to maintain visibility into AI applications, agents, connected systems, configurations and access permissions. Security teams use that information to assess risks and establish appropriate controls.
Once security professionals define policies and determine which changes can be handled automatically, Vero implements approved controls, coordinates remediation with the responsible parties and verifies completion.
When changes to the enterprise AI environment require a new risk assessment, the platform presents its analysis and recommended action to the relevant security professional.
Enterprise AI security controls across agents and infrastructure
A single enterprise security policy can require numerous technical controls across different applications, identities and infrastructure components.
One Fortune 1000 customer began deploying Vero with a policy restricting connections between AI agents and corporate code repositories, as well as code execution privileges, exclusively to developers.
Within minutes, Vero converted that policy into more than 15 security controls covering coding agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, skills, identities and runtime actions, automatically implementing them across the organization.
The platform continuously adjusts those controls as AI tools introduce new capabilities, maintaining enforcement of the original policy without requiring security teams to manually reconfigure each affected system.
“AI Security Engineering is becoming a core responsibility inside enterprise security organizations,” said Rona Segev, co-founder and managing partner at TLV Partners. “The professionals taking on that responsibility need technology designed for the pace and complexity of AI. Vero is bringing security expertise, continuous execution and runtime enforcement together in a platform built for how this new discipline needs to operate.”

Lawvek, an AI startup that helps enterprises recover vendor overcharges, missed rebates and service credits, has raised $550,000 in a pre-seed round led by Neon Fund, with participation from Inzas Ventures.
Advertisment
The San Francisco-based startup, co-founded by Amrit Khandelwal and Sudip Chhatui, said it will use the money to expand its enterprise customer base and strengthen the platform's ability to identify and recover money that vendors owe its customers.
What Lawvek does
Large companies negotiate prices, discounts and service commitments with their vendors. But the information needed to check whether a vendor has actually honoured those terms is usually spread across contracts, invoices, usage data and service records.
Lawvek's AI agents compare contract terms with billing, usage and service records. They flag price increases that go beyond agreed caps, volume discounts missing from invoices, and prepaid capacity that teams are on track to leave unused.
When a vendor owes a rebate or a service credit, Lawvek calculates the amount, gathers the evidence and files the claim on the customer's behalf. It then follows up with the vendor and checks that the credit shows up on an invoice or that the customer receives a refund.
Khandelwal, who is the CEO, explained the gap with an example from healthcare procurement.
"Say a health system negotiates a $2 rebate on every case of exam gloves if its hospitals buy 100,000 cases in a year. As soon as those hospitals reach the threshold, the supplier owes the health system $200,000. Every invoice can be correct, and the health system can still miss the entire rebate," Khandelwal said.
"Across industries, companies negotiate prices, discounts and service levels, yet still miss overcharges, earned rebates and credits for outages. Lawvek checks vendors' bills and performance against their contracts. When a vendor owes money, Lawvek gathers the evidence and follows up until the company receives a credit or refund," he added.
Lawvek points to McKinsey's estimate that unmet supplier commitments can cost large enterprises roughly 2% of their spending. For a company with $1 billion in annual spend, that works out to about $20 million a year.
The estimate appears in McKinsey's April 2025 report, "Mitigating procurement value leakage with generative AI", which described unfulfilled supplier obligations as leaking roughly 2% of spend, or about $40 million a year for a company spending $2 billion.
"The business world is full of blind spots, what's often referred to as localised ignorance. When we spoke with Lawvek's customers, we were struck by the scale of the problem and how little visibility enterprises have into it. We're pleased to back the team at this early stage as they build and validate the platform with enterprise customers," said Siddhartha Ahluwalia, partner at Neon Fund.
The founders and the investors
Co-founder Sudip Chhatui is a 2014 graduate of Netaji Subhas Institute of Technology (NSIT) and has spent over nine years in product growth and marketing roles, according to his LinkedIn profile. He previously worked with several Indian companies, including Curofy.
Lead investor Neon Fund was started by Ahluwalia and Nansi Mishra, the hosts of the 100x Entrepreneur podcast, which has since been rebranded as The Neon Show. The firm invests in early-stage B2B SaaS companies, with a focus on startups using AI.
In December 2025, Neon Fund announced the close of its third fund at $25 million. At the time, it had backed 12 startups from the fund and planned to back 13 more over the following year, with cheques of $500,000 to $1 million. Ahluwalia said the fund aims to help portfolio companies reach $10 million in annual recurring revenue within three years.
Neon Fund's portfolio includes Airmeet, Astra Security, CloudSek, InFeedo, SpotDraft, Highperformr and Zepic. Its portfolio company Requestly was acquired by BrowserStack in 2025.

Orthopaedic Startup OSSO Raises Rs 2.5 Crore in Extended Seed Round
Om Singh
| November 25 | Business Stories , Funding Feed
Share
Gurugram-based orthopaedic healthcare startup OSSO has raised Rs 2.5 crore in an extended seed funding round as it looks to strengthen its clinical capabilities and expand its footprint across the National Capital Region (NCR).
The company said the newly raised capital will support the development of its clinical services and expansion plans. The funding comes as OSSO builds an integrated healthcare model combining orthopaedic treatment, surgical capabilities and rehabilitation under one platform.
The extended round attracted investments from Rajeev Saraf, Tejinderpal Miglani, Priyanka Aggarwal, Akshay Varma and Vikas Bhadoria. They join the startup’s existing investors, including Umesh Kumar Agarwal from the Haldiram Family Office, Sahil Jindal and Blume Founders Fund, among others.
OSSO Expands Specialised Orthopaedic Services
Founded in 2025 by Kunal Kishore Dhawan and Avani Shukla , OSSO operates an integrated orthopaedic and rehabilitation centre. Its services cover clinical orthopaedics, physical medicine and rehabilitation (PM&R), physiotherapy, regenerative orthopaedics and sports injury care.
The startup has recently launched a centre focused on advanced orthopaedic procedures, with particular attention to joint preservation and sports injury treatment.
The facility will offer specialised procedures, including image-guided orthobiologic interventions, subchondral bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) and arthroscopic cartilage repair. Several of these treatments are minimally invasive and can be performed as day-care procedures.
The new centre will operate alongside OSSO’s flagship clinic in DLF Phase 4, Gurugram. The two facilities are intended to connect different stages of patient care, from diagnosis and procedures to rehabilitation.
Startup Plans 5-6 Additional Clinics in 2027
OSSO is targeting a wider NCR presence in 2027, with plans to establish five to six additional clinics and surgical units. The company also intends to onboard more orthopaedic surgeons as it develops a doctor-led healthcare platform.
Its expansion strategy centres on bringing specialised clinical services, surgical capabilities and rehabilitation together within a single network.
With the latest funding, OSSO plans to strengthen its clinical infrastructure while expanding access to specialised orthopaedic care across NCR. The planned additions in 2027 will mark the next phase of its effort to build a connected network of orthopaedic and rehabilitation facilities.

AidenAI, an enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) startup, has raised $32 million in a Series A funding round led by A91 Partners. The company was founded in 2023 by Srinivas Kamadi, a former Senior Vice President at Infosys.
Headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, AidenAI has a significant presence in India and operates across six countries. The company develops an AI builder platform to help enterprises build, deploy, and manage AI agents using their existing systems and AI models.

Its engineers work alongside enterprise clients to develop and implement AI solutions. The company also offers AiDAP, a platform for modernising legacy technology.

Industry leaders point to better data, faster learning cycles and closer connections between computation and experimentation as critical to translating AI-designed molecules into development decisions
LONDON , Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AI drug discovery is shifting from a race to design faster to a race to learn faster. As AI expands the speed and scale of design, the advantage increasingly lies with those who can turn those designs into validated biological evidence that informs decisions and improves models.
Highlights from GenScript’s London forum during Jefferies conference week.
Panelists and moderator participate in a discussion on the future of biotechnology during the GenScript forum.
Ray Chen, PhD, President of GenScript Life Science Group, speaks at the 2026 GenScript Biotech Global Forum in London.
That was the central proposition GenScript Biotech Corporation put to leaders from pharma, AI-native biotechnology, investment and science funding at the 2026 GenScript Biotech Global Forum London . Held during the week of the Jefferies London Healthcare Conference under the theme "AI, Biotech & Capital," the forum brought together executives from Eli Lilly and Company, Latent Labs, Sofinnova Partners, Basecamp Research, ARIA and GenScript to explore where AI is already creating scientific and economic value, where biology remains a limiting factor, and what evidence will be required as AI-generated possibilities move closer to development.
From AI Possibility to Biological Evidence
Panelists included Alan Belicha, PhD , Senior Director, Ecosystem Growth and Contributor Partnerships at Eli Lilly and Company; Simon Kohl, PhD , Founder and CEO of Latent Labs; Edward Kliphuis , Partner at Sofinnova Partners; Richard Pearce , Chief Business Officer at Basecamp Research; and Maximilian Sichrovsky, PhD , Science & Technology Lead at ARIA. GenScript was represented by Ray Chen, PhD , President of GenScript Life Science Group; Zhenyan Yan, PhD , Vice President of Corporate Development & Strategy; and Aylin Kosova Bilgin , Chief Marketing and Corporate Communications Officer.
Their discussion highlighted three forces shaping the next phase of AI-enabled drug discovery:
AI is moving into harder biology. Kohl described how quickly AI-enabled protein design is evolving, with the field moving beyond binding toward more complex modalities and questions of developability. Even with that progress, he said, the critical gap lies between generating a promising binder and developing a candidate a company is prepared to advance toward the clinic. Closing it requires addressing biological properties that are harder to model and more difficult to characterize experimentally. "This is all about building AI platforms that advance our partners' portfolios, our partners' programs," added Kohl. "Increasingly, we're betting on both building generative models and the agents around them to create end-to-end workflows. I think that's the exciting moment in time. It feels a lot like what GPT-3 felt like in language. That's what this field is now undergoing, and we couldn't be more excited for what's to come over the next one to two years."
Data quality and biological relevance are becoming more important. Panelists pointed to two related gaps: the need for datasets that support biologically relevant predictions, rather than simply more data, and the need for people who can bridge AI and wet-lab biology. As models take on harder biological questions, closer connections between dataset design, experimentation and computation will be critical to generating evidence that improves predictions and informs development decisions.
Capital follows evidence, not design volume. Pearce noted that AI is becoming effective at specific discovery tasks and could allow companies to reach the clinic with less capital than a traditional biotech would need. Long-term value, however, will depend on whether promising molecules can progress beyond design and through development, where biological and ultimately clinical evidence determines which ones move forward. As candidate generation accelerates, the evidence behind each candidate becomes more consequential in determining where development resources and capital are committed. "Ultimately, we're all paying for healthcare, and healthcare costs keep going up. And most development costs are actually going toward drugs that fail; the industry needs to think differently so that environment can change," Pearce added. "I think we're at the point where, with a better understanding of patient biology and stratification, new business models will evolve. Compared to other industries that have changed business models, the pharma industry is still doing the same thing it did 70 years ago: discovering a compound, doing a clinical trial, and hoping it works. In 20 years' time, I think that will have changed – and we will know that a new therapy works for a specific individual."
Turning Faster Design into Faster Learning
For GenScript, these themes converge around learning velocity: connecting AI-driven design with synthesis, expression, biological testing and usable data to shorten the path from computational possibility to experimental evidence. As discovery cycles accelerate, researchers also need the scientific depth and biological context to interpret that evidence and make informed development decisions.
The shift is already reflected in GenScript's AI drug discovery (AIDD) business, which doubled year over year to $37.8 million in revenue in the first half of 2026 .
